wacc.formula: WACC = wₑ × kₑ + w_d × k_d × (1 − t);  kₑ = r_f + β × ERP
steps: β (Blume-adjusted) = 0.67 × raw β 1.31 + 0.33 = 1.21  (104 weekly returns vs SPY, R² 0.20)
k_d = 7.10%  (10-year Treasury + 2% (no rate on file)); after tax 7.10% × (1 − 35%) = 4.61%

methods.formula: FCFF = EBIT × (1 − t) + D&A − capex − ΔWC;  EV = Σ FCFF/(1+WACC)^t + TV/(1+WACC)^5;  TV = NOPAT₆ × (1 − g ÷ ROIC) ÷ (WACC − g);  value = (EV − debt + cash − claims) ÷ shares
steps: growth by year -4%, -3%, -1%, -0%, 1%; EBIT margin 2.8%; D&A 3.2% of revenue; capex 3.2%, 3.2%, 3.2%, 3.2%, 3.2% of revenue; ΔWC 10% of each revenue increase

methods.formula: Graham number = √(22.5 × EPS × book value per share);  22.5 = a P/E of 15 × a P/B of 1.5
inputs: SEC XBRL frames: diluted weighted-average shares
assumptions: Benjamin Graham, The Intelligent Investor (1949; 1973 edition, ch. 14)
methods.fit: It has positive earnings and book value, the two things Graham asked a defensive investor to pay for — and to pay little for.

methods.formula: Value = EPS × (8.5 + 2g) × 4.4 ÷ Y;  g = expected yearly growth in percent, Y = the AAA corporate yield today
steps: g = 70.4% → capped to 15.0% (analysts' next-year EPS growth (3 analysts))
inputs: FRED DAAA (via the Debt & rates module)
assumptions: the P/E of a company that does not grow
the AAA yield when Graham set the formula
an assumption: the formula overstates value at high growth
methods.fit: It has positive earnings and a growth estimate; the formula prices that growth against today's AAA bond yield.

methods.formula: Fair P/E = growth + dividend yield, in percent (5–40);  value = EPS × fair P/E;  PEGY = P/E ÷ (growth + yield)
steps: growth 70.4% → 35.0% (analysts' next-year EPS growth (3 analysts)); dividend yield 4.8%
today P/E 14.3 → PEGY 0.36 (below 1: cheap for its growth, above 2: dear)
assumptions: Peter Lynch, One Up on Wall Street (1989)
a rule of thumb, not a model of cash flows
analysts look one or two years ahead; Lynch meant several
methods.fit: It has positive earnings and a growth rate, so its P/E can be set against the growth and yield it delivers.

methods.formula: Net current asset value per share = (current assets − total liabilities − other claims) ÷ shares;  a net-net trades below two-thirds of it
inputs: SEC XBRL frames: diluted weighted-average shares
assumptions: Fixed assets, goodwill, the business itself
Graham, Security Analysis (1934): a liquidation floor
methods.fit: Its current assets and liabilities are on file. Net-nets are rare among large companies; a positive figure is a floor that ignores everything the business owns beyond working capital.

methods.formula: EPV = adjusted earnings ÷ WACC − net debt;  adjusted earnings = normalized EBIT × (1 − t) + D&A − maintenance capex;  normalized EBIT = average margin × revenue
steps: normalized EBIT = 2.8% × $1.11B = $31.14M  (the last four quarters' EBIT margin (fewer than three years on file))
maintenance capex = $35.26M  (capex $35.26M − growth capex (PP&E $173.3M ÷ revenue × revenue gain $0 = $0))
assumptions: the business as it is, forever
methods.fit: It earns an operating profit over the cycle; EPV values that profit as if it never grew, which shows how much of the price is a bet on growth.

methods.formula: FCFE = net income − (1 − d) × (capex − D&A + ΔWC);  value = Σ FCFE ÷ (1 + kₑ)ᵗ + terminal ÷ (1 + kₑ)⁵;  terminal = net income₆ × (1 − g ÷ ROE) ÷ (kₑ − g)
steps: net margin 2.2%; d (debt share of capital) = 0%; growth -4%, -3%, -1%, -0%, 1%
assumptions: its own growth fading to terminal
methods.fit: It is profitable with positive equity, so the cash left for shareholders after reinvestment and borrowing can be projected.

methods.formula: ln(EV/Sales) = a + b₁ × growth + b₂ × ln(operating margin, at least 0.5%) + b₃ × loss flag + b₄ × ln(revenue, $B) + sector effect;  value = (fitted EV/Sales × revenue − net debt) ÷ shares
inputs: last four quarters vs the four before
assumptions: every covered non-financial company with revenue ≥ $50M, today; ridge λ = 1
methods.fit: It is a non-financial company with revenue on file, so the multiple the market pays companies with its growth, margin, size and sector applies.

methods.formula: Value = D₀ × [(1 + g_L) + H × (g_S − g_L)] ÷ (kₑ − g_L);  growth falls in a straight line from g_S to g_L over 2H years
inputs: SEC XBRL frames: diluted weighted-average shares
assumptions: an assumption: dividends rarely grow faster for a decade
methods.fit: It pays a dividend whose growth is likely to slow from today's pace to the economy's, which the H-model spreads over ten years.
